segments.title: Builth at the River Wye crossing
segments.summary: The opening places Builth Castle at a River Wye crossing between northern and southern Wales, where geography still explains the site despite the loss of its masonry.
segments.body: The surviving earthworks make more sense when set against the River Wye. Builth guarded a critical crossing between northern and southern Wales. In 1277 Edward I considered the surrounding country comparatively secure because local men were loyal and supplied a large share of his forces in Wales. Their loyalty gave the king a reason to protect their lands, so the crossing explains why a castle was useful even in friendly territory.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces Builth Castle, notes that mostly earthworks survive, and identifies the River Wye crossing.
The transcript describes the crossing between northern and southern Wales, local loyalty to Edward, and the need to protect those lands.

segments.title: Marcher and Welsh claims before Edward I
segments.summary: The older motte-and-bailey passed among Norman, Marcher, and Welsh claimants before Llywelyn ap Gruffudd destroyed it in 1260.
segments.body: Edward I inherited a site with a long frontier history. An earlier motte-and-bailey had two baileys and another boundary wall. Norman, Marcher, and Welsh lords fought over it, intermarried, and based some claims on inheritance through marriage. The castle changed hands and was modified several times before Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took and destroyed it in 1260, during Henry III's reign. Builth's history shows the Welsh Marches as a region of overlapping lordship and family claims rather than a clean political boundary.

evidence.note: The transcript says Builth had a pre-existing motte-and-bailey castle with two baileys and a further boundary wall.
The transcript describes Norman, Marcher, and Welsh lords fighting, intermarrying, and claiming the castle by inheritance.
The transcript says Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took and destroyed the castle in 1260.

segments.title: Edward I's cheap unfinished rebuild
segments.summary: Edward I's rebuild treats Builth as a blank slate, reuses the earthworks to limit cost, and remains unfinished when the wider Welsh threat changes.
segments.body: Builth never became one of the showpiece Edwardian castles. Edward treated the destroyed predecessor as a blank slate and began work in May 1277, but construction stopped unfinished in August 1282 because money ran short. The likely reason for abandoning further work was that Llywelyn ap Gruffudd had been killed and Edward no longer felt the same need to pay for a stronger castle. Existing earthworks kept the cost below 1,700 pounds, making Builth comparatively cheap. The decision to stop followed the changing threat and available money, while the inherited earthworks had already limited the cost.

evidence.note: The transcript says Edward I considered the site a blank slate, began work in May 1277, and left the original castle unfinished in August 1282 for lack of money.
The transcript links the halt to reduced need after Llywelyn ap Gruffudd's death and says the existing earthworks kept costs under 1700 pounds.

segments.title: The unfinished castle proves defensible
segments.summary: Madog ap Llywelyn's revolt tests Builth in 1294, but the unfinished castle holds and remains useful enough for a royal grant and Roger Mortimer's castellanship.
segments.body: Builth's unfinished state did not prevent it from working as a fortress. Forces in Madog ap Llywelyn's revolt besieged the castle in 1294 but failed to take it. Edward I gave Builth to his son Edward in 1301 to help organise and support the territory. Roger Mortimer served as castellan from 1310 to 1315. The castle continued to carry defensive and administrative value despite the limited investment in its fabric.

evidence.note: The transcript says Madog ap Llywelyn's revolt besieged but did not take Builth, Edward granted it to his son in 1301, and Roger Mortimer served as castellan from 1310 to 1315.

segments.title: Mortimer, Isabella, and Edward III
segments.summary: Builth's ownership becomes entangled with Isabella, Roger Mortimer, Edward II's fall, and Edward III's recovery of royal authority.
segments.body: Edward II gave Builth to his wife Isabella, who leased it to Roger Mortimer and thereby established their connection. Mortimer later became Isabella's lover and supported her coup against Edward II, which ended with the deposed king's death. When Edward III reached adulthood in 1330, he arranged the capture of Isabella and Mortimer, had Mortimer executed for treason, and seized his properties. Gilbert Talbot, the Justiciar of South Wales, then took Builth.

evidence.note: The transcript says Edward II gave the castle to Isabella, who leased it to Roger Mortimer, and that Mortimer became Isabella's lover.
The transcript links Mortimer and Isabella to the coup against Edward II, then describes Edward III's capture of them and Mortimer's execution.
The transcript says Edward III seized Mortimer's properties and Builth was taken by Gilbert Talbot, Justiciar of South Wales.

segments.title: Alice de Lacy and coerced lordship
segments.summary: Alice de Lacy's life grant and forced marriage to Hugh de Freyne show how personal vulnerability could redirect a strategically useful lordship.
segments.body: Edward III rewarded Alice de Lacy and her second husband, Eubulus le Strange, after their assistance during his takeover. They received Builth for life, linking the castle to loyalty at the start of the new reign. After Eubulus died, Hugh de Freyne forced Alice into marriage and thereby gained recognition as lord of Builth. The act was considered unacceptable even then, but Alice lacked surviving family able to defend her and the king chose not to intervene. Her case shows how inheritance could be redirected when a politically exposed landholder had little protection.

evidence.note: The transcript covers Edward III's life grant to Alice de Lacy and Eubulus le Strange, Alice's coerced remarriage to Hugh de Freyne, the king's nonintervention, and Freyne's recognition as lord of Builth.

segments.title: The Black Prince's garrison right
segments.summary: The Black Prince rents Builth back to the Mortimers but retains wartime garrison rights later exercised during Owain Glyndwr's revolt.
segments.body: Alice de Lacy died childless in 1348, allowing Edward III to grant Builth to the Black Prince. In 1359 the prince restored a rental arrangement with the still-powerful Mortimer family but kept the right to garrison the castle in wartime. That retained military authority mattered when Owain Glyndwr's forces attacked in the early fifteenth century. Sir John Oldcastle, described here as an apparent inspiration for Shakespeare's Falstaff, commanded the garrison. Repairs costing 400 pounds in 1409 show the crown still spending enough to keep the site serviceable after the crisis.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the grant to the Black Prince, the Mortimer rental with retained wartime garrison rights, Glyndwr's attack, Sir John Oldcastle's command, and the 1409 repair.

segments.title: Builth returns to the Tudor crown
segments.summary: The Wars of the Roses end the Mortimer rental, while Yorkist inheritance and Elizabeth of York's marriage carry Builth back into Tudor royal hands.
segments.body: Richard of York's claim to the crown during the Wars of the Roses ended the final Mortimer rental. After the deaths and inheritances that followed, Elizabeth of York became the relevant heir. Her marriage to the Lancastrian claimant Henry VII returned Builth to royal hands. In November 1493 the site was re-established as a Marcher lordship for their son Arthur. Arthur died childless in 1502, ending that attempt to place the lordship in a royal household.

evidence.note: The transcript ends the Mortimer rental during the Wars of the Roses, follows Elizabeth of York's marriage to Henry VII, and describes the Marcher lordship created for Arthur in 1493 before his childless death.

segments.title: Fire and stone robbing erase the castle
segments.summary: Fire during Henry VIII's reign and local reuse of the ruins explain why Builth survives mainly as earthworks rather than visible masonry.
segments.body: Builth burned during Henry VIII's reign. Local people then quarried the ruins for building stone, moving its masonry into nearby properties. No castle stonework remained visible by the time of the video, so photographs, terrain, and earthworks have to explain the site. The surviving landscape records both the medieval castle and its later dismantling.

evidence.note: The transcript says the castle burned during Henry VIII's reign, local people reused the ruins as building material, and no stonework now survives.

segments.title: A defensive castle at the edge of control
segments.summary: The closing argument uses Builth as an inland exception to the Ring of Iron: a river-edge defensive site protecting already controlled land.
segments.body: Builth tests the series' maritime argument because it lies far from the sea. The site stands beside a large river at the edge of English-controlled territory. The castle was more defensive than offensive: it protected the part of Wales already held rather than helping to conquer territory beyond it. Once that controlled area became secure, the reason for further investment weakened. The closing joke casts Builth as a poisoned chalice because so many of its owners met bad ends.

evidence.note: The transcript says Builth is far from the sea, a challenge to the maritime-power argument, but still at the edge of a large river and controlled territory.
The transcript says the castle is more defensive than offensive and is about defending the part of Wales already controlled.
The transcript jokes about the castle's unlucky ownership history after explaining its defensive purpose.
